The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an arbitrary complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), $I=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ a nonempty compact interval, $\hbar>0$, and $\mathcal H:I\to\mathcal B(H)$ a norm-continuous family of bounded self-adjoint operators. Put $A(t)=-i\mathcal H(t)/\hbar$ and $K=\sup_{t\in I}\|A(t)\|<\infty$. For every $s,t\in I$ define $U_0(t,s)=I_H$ and, recursively, the oriented Bochner integrals
$$U_{n+1}(t,s)=\int_s^t A(r)U_n(r,s)\,dr,$$
where $\int_s^t=-\int_t^s$ when $t<s$. Equivalently, for $s\le t$ these are the **latest-time-left** ordered integrals
$$U_n(t,s)=\Bigl(\frac{-i}{\hbar}\Bigr)^n\int_{s<t_1<\cdots<t_n<t}\mathcal H(t_n)\cdots\mathcal H(t_1)\,dt_1\cdots dt_n,$$
with the simplex integral meaning the nested integral with $t_n$ outermost and $t_1$ innermost. For arbitrary $s,t$ its unambiguous nested form is $\int_s^t dr_1\int_s^{r_1}dr_2\cdots\int_s^{r_{n-1}}dr_n\,A(r_1)\cdots A(r_n)$. Then:

(a) $\|U_n(t,s)\|\le(K|t-s|)^n/n!$ for all $n\ge0$ and all $s,t\in I$.

(b) $U(t,s)=\sum_{n\ge0}U_n(t,s)$ converges in operator norm uniformly on $I\times I$, is jointly norm-continuous, satisfies $U(s,s)=I_H$, and obeys $\|U(t,s)-I_H\|\le e^{K|t-s|}-1$. In particular all original forward-time convergence claims hold.

(c) For every $s,t\in I$,
$$U(t,s)=I_H-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_s^t\mathcal H(r)U(r,s)\,dr.$$
For fixed $s$ this is the unique continuous $\mathcal B(H)$-valued solution on $I$. More generally, the solution with initial value $C\in\mathcal B(H)$ at $s$ is $U(t,s)C$. For $a<b$, the operator-norm derivatives are
$$\partial_tU(t,s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\mathcal H(t)U(t,s),\qquad \partial_sU(t,s)=+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(t,s)\mathcal H(s),$$
with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Therefore, for every $\psi\in H$, $U(t,s)\psi$ is strongly continuously differentiable in either variable and satisfies the same equations applied to $\psi$, with the common bounded-generator domain equal to all of $H$.

(d) Every $U(t,s)$ is unitary, $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)=U(t,s)^{-1}$, and
$$U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)\qquad(r,s,t\in I).$$
These conclusions include both orientations of the time interval and intervals containing positive and negative times. If $a=b$, all terms with $n\ge1$ vanish and $U(a,a)=I_H$; the derivative assertions then have no nontrivial interval on which to apply.

No separability hypothesis on $H$, invariant domain for an unbounded operator, differentiability of $\mathcal H$, spectral theorem or physical interpretation is required.

derivations.claim: On any compact interval, $H$ is a norm-continuous bounded self-adjoint family, so [F1] supplies the unique unitary propagator there. On overlapping compact intervals the propagators agree by uniqueness; hence $U(t,s)$ is consistently defined for all real $s,t$. For each fixed $t$, the curves $r\mapsto U(r+T,T)$ and $r\mapsto U(r,0)$ solve the same differential equation because $H(r+T)=H(r)$, and both equal $I_d$ at $r=0$. Uniqueness in [F1] gives $U(t+T,T)=U(t,0)$.

Put $M=U(T,0)$. By [F1], $M$ is unitary, so [F2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $v_j$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of modulus one. Write $\lambda_j=x_j+iy_j$; then $(x_j,-y_j)$ lies on the real unit circle. By [F3], choose $\theta_j\in[0,2\pi)$ with $x_j=\cos\theta_j$ and $-y_j=\sin\theta_j$, so $\lambda_j=e^{-i\theta_j}$. Set $\varepsilon_j=\hbar\theta_j/T$ and define $H_Fv_j=\varepsilon_jv_j$. Each $\varepsilon_j$ is real, hence $H_F$ is Hermitian, and [F5] gives $e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}v_j=e^{-i\theta_j}v_j=\lambda_jv_j$. Equality on the basis proves $e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}=U(T,0)$.

If $\varepsilon'_j$ gives the same eigenphase as $\varepsilon_j$, then $\exp(-iT(\varepsilon'_j-\varepsilon_j)/\hbar)=1$. By [F4], $T(\varepsilon'_j-\varepsilon_j)/\hbar\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so $\varepsilon'_j-\varepsilon_j\in\hbar\omega\mathbb Z$. Conversely adding $n\hbar\omega$ multiplies the phase by $e^{-i2\pi n}=1$. Thus the class stated is independent of the real lift.

Define $P(t)=U(t,0)e^{itH_F/\hbar}$. Both factors are unitary by [F1] and [F5], so $P(t)$ is unitary, and the group law in [F5] gives $P(t)e^{-itH_F/\hbar}=U(t,0)$. By composition and step 1.1, $U(t+T,0)=U(t+T,T)U(T,0)=U(t,0)e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}$. Therefore
$$P(t+T)=U(t,0)e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}e^{i(t+T)H_F/\hbar}=U(t,0)e^{itH_F/\hbar}=P(t),$$
where the middle cancellation follows from [F5]. This proves the factorization and periodicity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Put
$D_\theta:=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(L)=e^{i\theta}u^*(0)\},\qquad
P_\theta u:=-i\,Du,$
with $H^1$ and the trace $u^*$ of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]
and [[lem-nrqm-intervals-integration-by-parts]] clause (b). Then:

(a) $D_\theta$ is dense in $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, $P_\theta$ is symmetric and
self-adjoint;

(b) the functions
$\varphi_n(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z)$
form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, each
$\varphi_n\in D_\theta$, and $P_\theta\varphi_n=\kappa_n\varphi_n$ with
$\kappa_n:=\frac{2\pi n+\theta}{L};$
the eigenvalues $\kappa_n$ are simple and
$\sigma(P_\theta)=\{\kappa_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$;

(c) $P_\theta$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of the symmetric operator
$P_\theta$ restricted to the finite linear span of the $\varphi_n$, and its
domain is exactly
$D_\theta=\Bigl\{\sum_nc_n\varphi_n:\sum_n\kappa_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix complex
scalars. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, bounded or
unbounded, and write $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of
Lebesgue (equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with the inner
product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_Iu\overline v$ linear in the first argument
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**First-order space.** Define
$H^1(I):=\{u\in L^2(I;\mathbb C):\ \text{the weak derivative }Du\text{ of the class }u\text{ exists and }Du\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)\},$
where $Du$ is the weak derivative of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]: a class
$Du\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;\mathbb C)$ with
$\int_Iu\,\varphi'=(-1)\int_I(Du)\varphi\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I),$
an identity that is choice-free
([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]). Equip
$H^1(I)$ with the sesquilinear form
$\langle u,v\rangle_{H^1}:=\int_Iu\overline v+\int_I(Du)\overline{Dv},$
whose associated norm is $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$;
the symbol $u'$ denotes the same weak derivative $Du$ throughout the page.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

**Endpoint-vanishing first-order space and the Dirichlet form.** For the
bounded interval $(0,L)$, $L>0$, define
$H^1_0(0,L):=\overline{C_c^\infty(0,L)}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{H^1}},$
the closure of the test functions in $H^1(0,L)$, and define the **Dirichlet
form** on it by $q_D[u]:=\|Du\|_{L^2(0,L)}^2=\int_0^L|Du|^2$.

**Elementary consequences, recorded for reuse.** Weak derivatives are unique
as locally integrable classes under Countable Choice, are additive and
$\mathbb C$-homogeneous, and classical derivatives of continuously
differentiable functions are weak derivatives. The cited published items
supply these facts, so $H^1(I)$ and $H^2(I)$ are well-defined linear
subspaces of $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$. No claim is made here that $H^1_0(0,L)$
equals the set of classes with vanishing endpoint values; that identification
is proved on this page from the trace estimates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and

principle is used for this assertion.

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,

2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix complex
scalars. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, bounded or
unbounded, and write $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of
Lebesgue (equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with the inner
product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_Iu\overline v$ linear in the first argument
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**First-order space.** Define
$H^1(I):=\{u\in L^2(I;\mathbb C):\ \text{the weak derivative }Du\text{ of the class }u\text{ exists and }Du\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)\},$
where $Du$ is the weak derivative of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]: a class
$Du\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;\mathbb C)$ with
$\int_Iu\,\varphi'=(-1)\int_I(Du)\varphi\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I),$
an identity that is choice-free
([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]). Equip
$H^1(I)$ with the sesquilinear form
$\langle u,v\rangle_{H^1}:=\int_Iu\overline v+\int_I(Du)\overline{Dv},$
whose associated norm is $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$;
the symbol $u'$ denotes the same weak derivative $Du$ throughout the page.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

**Endpoint-vanishing first-order space and the Dirichlet form.** For the
bounded interval $(0,L)$, $L>0$, define
$H^1_0(0,L):=\overline{C_c^\infty(0,L)}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{H^1}},$
the closure of the test functions in $H^1(0,L)$, and define the **Dirichlet
form** on it by $q_D[u]:=\|Du\|_{L^2(0,L)}^2=\int_0^L|Du|^2$.

**Elementary consequences, recorded for reuse.** Weak derivatives are unique
as locally integrable classes under Countable Choice, are additive and
$\mathbb C$-homogeneous, and classical derivatives of continuously
differentiable functions are weak derivatives. The cited published items
supply these facts, so $H^1(I)$ and $H^2(I)$ are well-defined linear
subspaces of $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$. No claim is made here that $H^1_0(0,L)$
equals the set of classes with vanishing endpoint values; that identification
is proved on this page from the trace estimates.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
